cards.title: Elusive right
cards.author: editorial
cards.why: It outlines Pakistan's official foreign policy stance on global governance and self-determination, which is essential for Current Affairs and International Relations papers.
cards.summary: Pakistan is advocating at the United Nations for the universal application of the right to self-determination. The country argues that the UN Charter is often ignored, particularly concerning occupied territories like Palestine and Kashmir. Pakistan also seeks reforms to the UN Security Council, including limiting or abolishing the veto power to ensure global democracy.
key_facts: Pakistan introduced a draft resolution titled 'Universal Realization of the Right to Self-Determination'.
Pakistan initiated UN Security Council Resolution 2788 in July 2025 regarding the peaceful settlement of disputes.
Pakistan officially opposes the expansion of permanent membership in the UN Security Council.
Pakistan advocates for the abolition or restriction of veto powers in the UN Security Council.

vocab.meaning: An action that violates a law or treaty.
A group leading the way in new developments or ideas.

text: Pakistan, as an ardent advocate of the right to self-determination, has called for the universal application of the spirit of freeing humanity from colonial constraints. While introducing a draft resolution titled "Universal Realization of the Right to Self-Determination", Pakistan's Permanent Representative to the United Nations, Ambassador Syed Haider Shah, made a coherent case - invoking the conscience of the international community to move beyond academic discourse and implement the UN Charter, which ironically remains unfulfilled in contravention of the stated principles of international law. That is because the sovereignty of states is, unfortunately, treated unequally, and there is no dearth of communities still longing for their fundamental rights to freedom of expression, speech and independence. Many remain under foreign occupation to this day, with the subjugated peoples of Palestine and Kashmir standing as prime examples of state repression. In July 2025, as President of the UNSC, Pakistan also initiated Resolution 2788 on "Strengthening Mechanisms for the Peaceful Settlement of Disputes", which was adopted unanimously. Likewise, Pakistan has remained at the vanguard of countries arguing that the world body is in dire need of reform - specifically, that the veto power should either be abolished or its use restricted under an agreed protocol in the interest of international peace and security. Pakistan also opposes any expansion of the UNSC's permanent membership. This entire vision that Pakistan advocates at the world body is primarily meant to democratise the institution - as envisioned at its inception in 1945 - and to ensure that the right to self-determination, as a cardinal principle, is universally realised. Pakistan's envoy aptly reminded the world that in several situations across the world, the legitimate aspirations of peoples continue to be met with "military oppression, excessive use of force, extrajudicial killings, arbitrary detentions, enforced disappearances, and attempts at demographic engineering". This serves as a powerful call for introspection and decisive action to uphold basic human rights.

cards.title: Another life lost to rabies
cards.author: editorial
cards.why: This issue highlights critical gaps in public health governance and urban management in Pakistan, relevant to policy-making essays.
cards.summary: The death of a student from rabies in Islamabad highlights systemic failures in managing stray dog populations and medical treatment efficacy. Despite high annual infection rates, current interventions remain fragmented and ineffective. Experts advocate for moving away from mass culling toward systematic vaccination and birth control programs for stray animals.
key_facts: Gallup Pakistan Digital Analytics reports approximately 300,000 dog-bite cases annually.
The Medical Microbiology and Infectious Diseases Society of Pakistan estimates 2,000 to 5,000 rabies deaths per year.
Recommended strategies include trap-neuter-vaccinate-return (TNVR) and animal birth control programs.

vocab.meaning: Failed to resist an illness or died from it.
The ability to produce a desired result.

text: Another preventable tragedy has claimed a life in Pakistan - this time in Islamabad, the country's capital and best-managed city. Sufyan Rashid Abbasi, a student at the International Islamic University Islamabad and the only brother of five sisters, died earlier this week after being bitten by a stray dog outside his campus hostel last month. What is even more alarming is that the 22-year-old succumbed despite receiving an initial anti-rabies vaccine at Rawalpindi's Holy Family Hospital following the attack. The young man's death raises troubling questions about both the adequacy of his post-exposure treatment and the university administration's inaction over stray dogs on campus, despite students having reportedly flagged the hazard around the hostels before the attack. Losing a student to a cent per cent preventable disease within an institution meant to provide a safe learning environment is deeply concerning. This is hardly an isolated incident. Far too many lives have been lost across the country - in far too many cities to list. Data compiled by Gallup Pakistan Digital Analytics estimates roughly 300,000 reported dog-bite cases per year nationwide, while the Medical Microbiology and Infectious Diseases Society of Pakistan estimates between 2,000 and 5,000 rabies-related deaths annually. While piecemeal measures, including mass culling, have been taken to address the crisis, far more comprehensive interventions are needed. Authorities should implement sustained trap-neuter-vaccinate-return (TNVR) and animal birth control programmes, along with regular mass vaccination of stray dogs. Equally urgent is safeguarding the efficacy of post-exposure treatment. Given that Sufyan died despite receiving an initial vaccine dose, health regulators must enforce strict quality control and cold-chain monitoring to eliminate substandard or compromised vaccines, while ensuring that public hospitals maintain adequate stocks of both anti-rabies vaccines and Rabies Immunoglobulin for severe bites. Until the relevant authorities treat rabies as the public health emergency it is, preventable tragedies like Sufyan's will continue to repeat themselves.
